The sum of the digits must be \(13\).  

If the palindrome has an even number of digits, each digit appears twice, so the total sum would be even – impossible.  
Hence only odd–length palindromes can occur.

Let the length be \(2k+1\) \((k\ge 0)\).  
Write the palindrome as  

\[
a_1a_2\ldots a_k\,m\,a_k\ldots a_2a_1 ,
\]

where each \(a_i\) and \(m\) are digits from \(1\) to \(9\).  
The digit sum is  

\[
2(a_1+\cdots +a_k)+m=13 .
\]

Thus \(m\) must be odd: \(m\in\{1,3,5,7,9\}\).  
For each such \(m\) set \(S=\dfrac{13-m}{2}\). Then

\[
a_1+\cdots +a_k=S,
\qquad
1\le a_i\le 9 .
\]

The possible \((m,S)\) pairs are  

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
m & S\\\hline
9&2\\
7&3\\
5&4\\
3&5\\
1&6
\end{array}
\]

Now we count, for each \(k\) (\(1\le k\le 6\), because \(2k+1\le13\) is needed), the number of ordered \(k\)-tuples \((a_1,\dots ,a_k)\) of digits \(1\!-\!9\) summing to each admissible \(S\).

Denote \(f(k,S)\) = # of ordered \(k\)-tuples of \(\{1,\dots ,9\}\) with sum \(S\).

\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccc}
k & f(k,2) & f(k,3) & f(k,4) & f(k,5) & f(k,6)\\\hline
1&1&1&1&1&1\\
2&1&2&3&4&5\\
3&0&1&3&6&10\\
4&0&0&1&4&10\\
5&0&0&0&1&5\\
6&0&0&0&0&1
\end{array}
\]

(These are obtained by standard “stars‑and‑bars’’ with the lower bound \(1\).)

Now sum the contributions, ignoring the impossible cases where \(S<k\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
k=1:&\;1+1+1+1+1 =5\\
k=2:&\;1+2+3+4+5 =15\\
k=3:&\;1+3+6+10 =20\\
k=4:&\;1+4+10 =15\\
k=5:&\;1+5 =6\\
k=6:&\;1 =1
\end{aligned}
\]

Adding them gives  

\[
5+15+20+15+6+1 = 62 .
\]

Thus there are \(\boxed{62}\) positive integer palindromes in base \(10\) with no zero digits whose digits sum to \(13\).
